questions.q: What kind of SSRS data region is WorkOrderProductionSummary.rdl built as, and why?
options: A Matrix, because it groups FactWorkOrder rows by Product and summarizes them into one line per product
A List, because it needs to show every work order row individually with no grouping
A Chart, because the report has no numeric measures at all
A Gauge, because it only shows a single current value
questions.explain: Grouping by Product turns hundreds of individual FactWorkOrder rows into one summary line per product — exactly what a Matrix data region is for.

questions.q: Why does the scrap-rate expression wrap both fields in Sum(), as in =Sum(Fields!ScrappedQty.Value) / Sum(Fields!OrderQty.Value)?
options: Without Sum(), the expression divides one detail row's values instead of the group's totals, producing a wrong number for any group with more than one row
Sum() is required syntax for every SSRS expression, regardless of what it computes
It converts the result from a percentage to a decimal
It prevents the report from running against more than one product
questions.explain: The report is grouped by Product; the scrap rate that matters is the product's overall rate across all its work orders, which requires summing both quantities at the group level before dividing.

questions.q: Where should the Scrap Rate expression's percentage formatting be applied?
options: In the text box's Number formatting (Percentage), not baked into the expression itself
By multiplying the expression by 100 and concatenating a "%" string inside the expression
It cannot be formatted as a percentage in SSRS at all
By renaming the ScrappedQty field to include "Percent" in its name
questions.explain: Expressions compute the value; formatting decides how it displays — the same separation SSRS Development's own formatting lessons teach.

questions.q: What does adding a ProductName report parameter, defaulted to "(All)" via a Select Parameter Values dataset, accomplish?
options: The report opens fully populated across every product, and a user can narrow it to one product only when they want to
It permanently deletes every product except the one selected from the underlying warehouse table
It changes the grain of dw.FactWorkOrder from one row per work order to one row per product
It removes the need for the report to connect to a data source at all
questions.explain: A parameter filters what a report shows without changing the underlying query's shape — defaulting to "(All)" keeps the report useful before anyone touches the parameter.

questions.q: Which three FactWorkOrder measures does WorkOrderProductionSummary.rdl sum per product?
options: OrderQty, StockedQty, and ScrappedQty
StartDateKey, EndDateKey, and DueDateKey
WorkOrderKey, ProductKey, and ScrapReasonKey
ProductName, ScrapReasonName, and DateKey
questions.explain: OrderQty, StockedQty, and ScrappedQty are the fact table's numeric measures — the date keys and surrogate keys are role-playing dimension links and identifiers, not the summed values.
